title: The Christmas Stock Is Already Paid For. The Cash It Returns Won't Land Until January.
linkedin:
Most Christmas stock is already paid for.

The sales that are supposed to repay it haven't started yet, and won't fully land until deep into December, sometimes January.

Here's the pattern we see across East Coast retail, hospitality and wholesale businesses this time of year. Stock gets ordered and paid for on thirty or sixty day terms weeks before Christmas trading even begins. The cash goes out early.

The matching sales come back later, and once they do, EFTPOS settlement timing, wholesale debtor terms or a straight lag between a sale and a bank deposit stretches the gap even further.

A bigger December doesn't close this gap. It widens it. More stock bought to meet more demand means more cash leaving the account earlier, unless the underlying payment and settlement terms move with it.

The businesses that trade through December comfortably are the ones who size this gap in dollar terms before the final stock order goes in, not the ones hoping trading volume will quietly cover it.

Three things worth checking before that final order: the actual payment terms you are on, not the ones you've always assumed, whether settlement timing has shifted with any recent payment processor change, and whether casual wages for the extra trading days are mapped against when the matching sales actually bank.

None of this is a bookkeeping gap. It's a commercial question sitting one layer above the ledger, worth asking now rather than in late January when the account runs tight.

For East Coast retail, hospitality and wholesale businesses, most of the stock for the Christmas trading period is already ordered and paid for by mid November. That spend typically sits on thirty or sixty day supplier terms, and those terms often run out before a single extra Christmas sale has come through the till.

The sales that are supposed to repay that spend mostly land in a narrow window between late November and Christmas Eve, and once they do, there is usually still a short delay before that money actually clears, through EFTPOS settlement timing, wholesale debtor terms, or redemption timing on gift cards and vouchers.

A busier December does not automatically close this gap. More stock bought to meet more demand means more cash leaving the account earlier, so the timing gap often gets wider in a strong trading month, not smaller, unless supplier terms or settlement speed move with it.

Before placing a final Christmas stock order, it is worth checking the actual payment terms on that order, whether settlement timing has shifted with any recent change in payment processor, and whether casual wages for extra trading days are mapped against when the matching sales genuinely bank.
